title: Late reports, late registration and lobbying disclosed after the decision
question: How often are lobbyists’ monthly reports late, how often does a lobbyist report contacts made before registering, and how much lobbying on a Board file was disclosed only after the Board’s final vote on it?
finding: Of 32,251 original monthly reports, 3,039 (9.4%) were received after the 15th of the following month and 409 more than thirty days after it. 178 contacts about 25 Board files were first disclosed in a late report that arrived after the Board’s final vote on the file. 55 lobbyists who registered from 2019 on reported 233 contacts dated more than a week before their registration. 24 permit consultants ticked the box saying they also qualify as lobbyists, and 22 of those names are found among registered lobbyists. The Ethics Commission’s penalty list shows 12 lobbying cases since 2012, with penalties of $58,168 in all.
how: The deadline and the registration rule are taken from two Ethics Commission stipulations on file (“By the 15th day of every month, lobbyists are required to publicly disclose”; lobbyists must “register no later than five business days after qualifying as a lobbyist”). Lateness is measured on the first version of each monthly report: the date received against the 15th of the month after the period. A contact is “disclosed after the final vote” when it names a Board file by number, is dated on or before the day of the Board’s final roll call on that file, and sits in a report whose first version was late and arrived after that day. The day of the vote is read from the Board’s roll-call pages for 21 of the 25 files; where no final roll call is on disk (a vote before 2015, or one that neither the vote page nor the minutes records member by member) the date the file is recorded as passed is used. That recorded date falls after the final roll call, typically by 9 days, and for 3 of these files the Board’s status record does not show passage although the roll-call page records a final vote that carried; measured by the recorded date alone, as this screen did before the roll calls were on disk, the count is 127 contacts on 23 files. Registration dates come from the Lobbyist Directory. Its earliest date is 2018-01-03 although reports go back to 2010, so older registrations appear to carry the date they were moved to a new filing system; only registrations from 2019 are tested, and anyone active more than a year before their date is left out as an earlier registrant. Penalties are matched to lobbyists by name.
limits: A late report is a filing lapse, not concealment; many are a day or two late. The filing file shows when a report’s first version arrived, not what it said, so a contact added later by amendment looks earlier than it was disclosed, which makes these counts a floor. A contact dated before registration can be the very contact that made the person a lobbyist, which the rule allows within five business days; the week’s grace here is approximate. A permit consultant may be registered as a lobbyist under a different spelling or through a firm. Nothing here can show lobbying by people who never registered at all: that takes a complaint and an investigation, as in the cases listed under enforcement. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
